newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-Asia's benchmark Tapis at post Gulf War high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Asia's benchmark Tapis at post Gulf War high.

text.p: The price of Asia's benchmark Tapis crude oil reached its highest level since the Gulf War on Thursday, boosted by strong demand for light, low sulphur crude.
Malaysia's Tapis was offered by a producer at $24.00/$24.10 per barrel -- the highest level since the 1990/1991 Gulf War when price assessments reached $39.08.
A cocktail of factors is fuelling the rally, including strong fourth-quarter demand for crudes like Tapis, which are rich in middle distillate products, like gas oil and jet fuel, when refined.
"Prices are getting very strong and a lot is related to middle distillate demand. But there have been lots of other problems so that traders are scrambling for crude," one oil trader said.

The middle distillates demand is exacerbated by U.S. data that show distillate stocks in the energy hungry United States are running almost 19 million barrels below last year's levels and are only building slowly. That could create demand for Asian crude and products.
Traditionally, distillate stocks grow strongly as the fourth quarter winter season approaches and demand for heating grows.
But despite the seasonal factor, other ingredients are adding to the cocktail, crude traders said.
Reduced output from Indonesia's 90,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) light sweet Belida field -- as a floating storage vessel is moored -- is reducing available supplies.
Ongoing production problems at Australia's 115,000 barrels per day (bpd) light-sweet Cossack field, which at times has cut output to just 50,000 bpd, is another ingredient.
Rising refinery demand from South Korea is a further factor. The country's refining capacity is expected to grow to 2.44 million bpd in 1996 from 1.82 million in 1995.
As part of South Korea's expansion, Yukong Ltd, the country's largest oil refiner, is bringing a 200,000 bpd distillate unit to commercial production in early October.

In Indonesia, a 70,000 bpd basic refining unit is due to come on stream in November for a new petrochemical plant. The unit can only take very light crude oil in order to produce light distillates, like naphtha.
In addition, the strength of the Brent futures market, which is just below post Gulf War highs, is making West African crude oil too expensive to bring to Asia.
West African crudes often compete against Asia's light sweet grades and are priced against the North Sea Brent market.
The cocktail has transferred into higher prices for a range of light sweet crude oils, apart from just Tapis.

An oil major sold 500,000 barrels of mid October lifting Australian North West Shelf condensate at a premium of 60 cents above its Arun price benchmark. The condensate normally trades at a 30 or 40 cents premium.
A European major sold 600,000 barrels of late October lifting Australian Kutubu crude oil to China at a market premium of 18 cents pre barrel. Kutubu traded only last week at a discount of 30 cents.
A major sold 250,000 barrels of early November lifting Skua crude, which normally trades at parity to Tapis crude, at a premium of $1.05 to a trader.
